claim: Understanding changes in infectiousness during SARS-CoV-2 infections is critical to assess the effectiveness of public health measures such as contact tracing.
source: Understanding changes in infectiousness during SARS-COV-2 infections is critical to assess the effectiveness of public health measures such as contact tracing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background context, drawing on established knowledge about the importance of understanding disease dynamics for public health interventions.

claim: A novel mechanistic approach was developed to infer the infectiousness profile of SARS-CoV-2-infected individuals using data from known infector–infectee pairs.
source: Here, we develop a novel mechanistic approach to infer the infectiousness profile of SARS-COV-2-infected individuals using data from known infector–infectee pairs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The mechanistic method provides an improved fit to data from SARS-CoV-2 infector–infectee pairs compared to commonly used approaches.
source: The mechanistic method provides an improved fit to data from SARS-CoV-2 infector–infectee pairs compared to commonly used approaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by AIC comparisons presented in the Results section showing the variable infectiousness model had the best fit (ΔAIC = 0).

claim: The best-fitting model indicates a high proportion of presymptomatic transmissions.
source: Our best-fitting model indicates a high proportion of presymptomatic transmissions, with many transmissions occurring shortly before the infector develops symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by the posterior distribution analysis showing 65% (0.53–0.77) presymptomatic transmission for the variable infectiousness model.

claim: Many transmissions occur shortly before the infector develops symptoms.
source: Our best-fitting model indicates a high proportion of presymptomatic transmissions, with many transmissions occurring shortly before the infector develops symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2B showing the TOST distribution concentrated around symptom onset for the variable infectiousness model.

claim: High infectiousness immediately prior to symptom onset highlights the importance of continued contact tracing until effective vaccines have been distributed widely.
source: High infectiousness immediately prior to symptom onset highlights the importance of continued contact tracing until effective vaccines have been distributed widely, even if contacts from a short time window before symptom onset alone are traced.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis results showing high presymptomatic transmission and the contact tracing effectiveness calculations.

claim: The precise proportion of SARS-CoV-2 transmissions arising from non-symptomatic infectors remains uncertain.
source: The precise proportion of SARS-CoV-2 transmissions arising from non-symptomatic (either presymptomatic or asymptomatic) infectors, as well as from unreported infected hosts with only mild symptoms, remains uncertain (Buitrago-Garcia et al., 2020; Casey et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature indicating ongoing uncertainty in the field.

claim: Statistical models can be used to assess the relative contributions of presymptomatic and symptomatic transmission using data from infector–infectee transmission pairs.
source: Statistical models can be used to assess the relative contributions of presymptomatic and symptomatic transmission using data from infector–infectee transmission pairs (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Zhang, 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Tindale et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies that have used this approach.

claim: The generation time is the difference between the infection times of the infector and infectee.
source: the generation time (the difference between the infection times of the infector and infectee) (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b; Deng et al., 2020; Ganyani et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a standard epidemiological definition supported by citations.

claim: The serial interval is the difference between the symptom onset times of the infector and infectee.
source: the serial interval (the difference between the symptom onset times of the infector and infectee) (Ferretti et al., 2020b; Du et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a standard epidemiological definition supported by citations.

claim: The generation time distribution indicates the average infectiousness of a host at each time since infection.
source: The generation time and TOST distributions indicate the average infectiousness of a host at each time since infection and time since symptom onset, respectively (He et al., 2020; Fraser, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work establishing this relationship.

claim: The TOST distribution indicates the average infectiousness of a host at each time since symptom onset.
source: The generation time and TOST distributions indicate the average infectiousness of a host at each time since infection and time since symptom onset, respectively (He et al., 2020; Fraser, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work establishing this relationship.

claim: Generation time and TOST distributions are important for assessing the effectiveness of public health measures such as isolation and contact tracing.
source: These distributions are important for assessing the effectiveness of public health measures such as isolation (Ashcroft et al., 2021; Wells et al., 2021) and contact tracing (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Fraser et al., 2004; Davis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating the use of these distributions for evaluating interventions.

claim: Estimates of the SARS-CoV-2 generation time have typically involved an assumption that a host's infectiousness is independent of their symptom status.
source: Estimates of the SARS-CoV-2 generation time have typically involved an assumption that a host's infectiousness is independent of their symptom status (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Deng et al., 2020; Ganyani et al., 2020; Knight and Mishra, 2020; Lehtinen et al., 2021; Figure 1B, left).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The assumption that infectiousness is independent of symptom status is unjustified.
source: However, such an assumption is unjustified (Lehtinen et al., 2021; Bacallado et al., 2020) and can lead to a poor fit to data (Ferretti et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that have critiqued this assumption.

claim: The assumption that infectiousness is independent of symptom status can lead to a poor fit to data.
source: However, such an assumption is unjustified (Lehtinen et al., 2021; Bacallado et al., 2020) and can lead to a poor fit to data (Ferretti et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating poor model fit.

claim: The mechanistic approach was motivated by compartmental epidemic models with Gamma distributed stage durations.
source: This approach was motivated by compartmental epidemic models with Gamma distributed stage durations (Lloyd, 2009; Wearing et al., 2005) and changes in infectiousness during infection (Hethcote et al., 1991; Christofferson et al., 2014; Hart et al., 2019; Hart et al., 2020; Gatto et al., 2020; Aleta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling literature.

claim: The mechanistic approach was motivated by models with changes in infectiousness during infection.
source: This approach was motivated by compartmental epidemic models with Gamma distributed stage durations (Lloyd, 2009; Wearing et al., 2005) and changes in infectiousness during infection (Hethcote et al., 1991; Christofferson et al., 2014; Hart et al., 2019; Hart et al., 2020; Gatto et al., 2020; Aleta et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling literature.

claim: Four different models of infectiousness were considered in the study.
source: We considered four different models of infectiousness (see Materials and methods):
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design, with details provided in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Each model was fitted to data from 191 SARS-CoV-2 transmission pairs.
source: We fitted each model to data from 191 SARS-CoV-2 transmission pairs (Ferretti et al., 2020b; Figure 2—source data 1) obtained by combining data from five studies (Ferretti et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data used in the analysis, with citations to the source studies.

claim: The transmission pair data were obtained by combining data from five studies.
source: We fitted each model to data from 191 SARS-CoV-2 transmission pairs (Ferretti et al., 2020b; Figure 2—source data 1) obtained by combining data from five studies (Ferretti et al., 2020a; He et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data sources with specific citations.

claim: Data augmentation Markov chain Monte Carlo was used to account for uncertainty in the precise times of symptom appearance within the day of onset.
source: To account for uncertainty in the precise times of symptom appearance within the day of onset for the infector and infectee (Thompson, 2020), we used data augmentation Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC).
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology used, with a citation supporting the approach.

claim: The variable infectiousness model provided the best fit to the data with ΔAIC = 0.
source: The best fit to the data was obtained using the variable infectiousness model (ΔAIC = 0).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model comparison results based on AIC values.

claim: The constant infectiousness model gave the next best fit with ΔAIC = 1.3.
source: The constant infectiousness model gave the next best fit (ΔAIC = 1.3)
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model comparison results based on AIC values.

claim: The Ferretti model had ΔAIC = 5.1.
source: followed by the Ferretti model (ΔAIC = 5.1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model comparison results based on AIC values.

claim: The independent transmission and symptoms model fitted least well with ΔAIC = 38.9.
source: Finally, the model with the standard assumption of independent transmission and symptoms fitted least well (ΔAIC = 38.9).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the model comparison results based on AIC values.

claim: The predicted variability in the generation time between individuals was lower for the independent transmission and symptoms model compared to the other three models.
source: The predicted variability in the generation time between individuals was lower for the independent transmission and symptoms model compared to the other three models (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 2A showing the generation time distributions.

claim: The TOST distribution was most concentrated around the time of symptom onset for the best-fitting variable infectiousness model.
source: On the other hand, the TOST distribution was most concentrated around the time of symptom onset for the best-fitting variable infectiousness model, and least concentrated for the independent transmission and symptoms model (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be observed in Figure 2B showing the TOST distributions.

claim: In the best-fitting model, a decrease in infectiousness was inferred following symptom onset.
source: In the best-fitting model, a decrease in infectiousness was inferred following symptom onset, likely due to behavioural factors that reduce the transmission risk following symptom appearance (Manfredi and D'Onofrio, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the fitted model parameters and supported by a citation to literature on behavioral changes.

claim: The decrease in infectiousness following symptom onset is likely due to behavioural factors that reduce the transmission risk following symptom appearance.
source: In the best-fitting model, a decrease in infectiousness was inferred following symptom onset, likely due to behavioural factors that reduce the transmission risk following symptom appearance (Manfredi and D'Onofrio, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the model results, supported by a citation to relevant literature.

claim: The median proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.65 (0.53–0.77) under the variable infectiousness model.
source: The median (95% credible interval) proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.65 (0.53–0.77), 0.56 (0.50–0.62), 0.55 (0.48–0.62), and 0.49 (0.43–0.56) under the variable infectiousness model, constant infectiousness model, Ferretti model, and independent transmission and symptoms model, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the posterior estimates from the model fitting.

claim: The median proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.56 (0.50–0.62) under the constant infectiousness model.
source: The median (95% credible interval) proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.65 (0.53–0.77), 0.56 (0.50–0.62), 0.55 (0.48–0.62), and 0.49 (0.43–0.56) under the variable infectiousness model, constant infectiousness model, Ferretti model, and independent transmission and symptoms model, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the posterior estimates from the model fitting.

claim: The median proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.55 (0.48–0.62) under the Ferretti model.
source: The median (95% credible interval) proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.65 (0.53–0.77), 0.56 (0.50–0.62), 0.55 (0.48–0.62), and 0.49 (0.43–0.56) under the variable infectiousness model, constant infectiousness model, Ferretti model, and independent transmission and symptoms model, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the posterior estimates from the model fitting.

claim: The median proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.49 (0.43–0.56) under the independent transmission and symptoms model.
source: The median (95% credible interval) proportion of presymptomatic transmissions was 0.65 (0.53–0.77), 0.56 (0.50–0.62), 0.55 (0.48–0.62), and 0.49 (0.43–0.56) under the variable infectiousness model, constant infectiousness model, Ferretti model, and independent transmission and symptoms model, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the posterior estimates from the model fitting.

claim: The central estimate of 65% of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset using the best-fitting model is higher than estimated in most previous studies.
source: The central estimate of 65% of transmissions occurring prior to symptom onset using the best-fitting model is higher than estimated in most previous studies in which the generation time and/or TOST were estimated (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Ferretti et al., 2020b; He et al., 2020; Ashcroft et al., 2020).
evidence: This compares the current study's results to previous literature through citations.

claim: There is significant variation in estimates of the contribution of presymptomatic transmission in the wider literature, including estimates exceeding 65%.
source: In the wider literature, we note significant variation in estimates of the contribution of presymptomatic transmission (obtained under a range of different modelling assumptions), including estimates exceeding 65% (Casey et al., 2020; Tindale et al., 2020; Ganyani et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies with varying estimates.

claim: Under the variable infectiousness model, 23% (17–31%) of all transmissions that would be generated by a symptomatic host are prevented if the host is isolated one day after symptom onset.
source: Under the best-fitting variable infectiousness model, 23% (17–31%) of all transmissions that would be generated by a symptomatic host are prevented if the host is isolated one day after symptom onset (Figure 4A, blue).
evidence: This is calculated from the model and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Under the independent transmission and symptoms model, 38% (32–44%) of transmissions are prevented if the host is isolated one day after symptom onset.
source: This compares to a higher estimate of 38% (32–44%) with the standard independent transmission and symptoms assumption (Figure 4A, purple dashed)
evidence: This is calculated from the model and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The limited impact of isolation of symptomatic hosts alone under the variable infectiousness model highlights the need to also conduct contact tracing.
source: The limited impact of isolation of symptomatic hosts alone under the variable infectiousness model, which is due to the high predicted proportion of presymptomatic transmissions (Figure 3A), highlights the need to also conduct contact tracing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model results showing limited effectiveness of isolation alone.

claim: Under the variable infectiousness model, 69% (57–81%) of presymptomatic infectious contacts are identified if a contact elicitation window of 2 days before the index host develops symptoms is used.
source: The variable infectiousness model indicates that 69% (57–81%) of presymptomatic infectious contacts are identified if a contact elicitation window of (up to) 2 days before the index host develops symptoms is used (as in the UK [UK Government, 2021] and USA [Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021]), compared to only 49% (44–53%) for the independent transmission and symptoms model (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the model and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A contact elicitation window of 2 days is used in the UK and USA.
source: The variable infectiousness model indicates that 69% (57–81%) of presymptomatic infectious contacts are identified if a contact elicitation window of (up to) 2 days before the index host develops symptoms is used (as in the UK [UK Government, 2021] and USA [Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021])
evidence: This is supported by citations to UK and USA government guidance.

claim: Under the independent transmission and symptoms model, 49% (44–53%) of presymptomatic infectious contacts are identified with a 2-day contact elicitation window.
source: compared to only 49% (44–53%) for the independent transmission and symptoms model (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is calculated from the model and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: If the contact elicitation window is extended to 4 days, then 93% (88–97%) of presymptomatic infectious contacts are identified under the variable infectiousness model.
source: If the contact elicitation window is extended to 4 days, then 93% (88–97%) of presymptomatic infectious contacts are identified under the variable infectiousness model.
evidence: This is calculated from the model.

claim: Choosing a longer contact elicitation window requires more contacts to be traced, many of whom are likely to be uninfected.
source: However, while choosing a longer contact elicitation window ensures more infected contacts are identified, it also requires more contacts to be traced, many of whom are likely to be uninfected.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the practical implications of extending the contact elicitation window.

claim: Index cases are expected to be less infectious at longer time periods prior to symptom onset.
source: This effect is enhanced by the fact that index cases are expected to be less infectious at longer time periods prior to symptom onset (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is inferred from the TOST distribution shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Under the variable infectiousness model, 71% of onward transmissions from a contact would be prevented if there is a total delay of 4 days between the contact being infected and isolated.
source: Under the variable infectiousness model, 71% of onward transmissions from the contact would then be expected to be prevented after this delay (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is calculated from the model for a specific scenario and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: For a contact that occurred 4 days before the index host developed symptoms, only 41% of the contact's onward infections would be expected to be prevented with a 6-day total delay.
source: In contrast, for an infectious contact that occurred 4 days before the index host developed symptoms (so that the total delay between the contact being infected and isolated is 6 days, assuming that the contact elicitation window is at least 4 days so the contact is traced), only 41% of the contact's onward infections would be expected to be prevented (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is calculated from the model for a specific scenario and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The mechanistic framework provides an improved fit to data compared to a model predicated on the assumption that infectiousness is independent of symptoms.
source: Here, we have considered a range of approaches for estimating epidemiological time periods using data from SARS-CoV-2 infector–infectee transmission pairs. Our mechanistic framework provides an improved fit to data compared to a model predicated on the assumption that infectiousness is independent of symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by the AIC comparison showing the mechanistic models fit better than the independent transmission and symptoms model.

claim: The assumption that infectiousness is independent of symptoms underlies most previous studies in which the SARS-CoV-2 generation time distribution has been estimated.
source: Despite neglecting potential relationships between viral shedding and symptoms, as well as behavioural changes in response to symptoms (Manfredi and D'Onofrio, 2013), that assumption underlies most previous studies in which the SARS-COV-2 generation time distribution has been estimated (Ferretti et al., 2020a; Deng et al., 2020; Ganyani et al., 2020; Knight and Mishra, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Some previous studies have considered an alternative assumption that infectiousness depends only on the time since symptom onset, independent of the time of infection.
source: Some previous studies in which the generation time (Ferretti et al., 2020b; Davis et al., 2020) and/or TOST distributions (Ferretti et al., 2020b; He et al., 2020; Ashcroft et al., 2020) were estimated have considered an alternative assumption that infectiousness depends only on the time since symptom onset, independent of the time of infection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If the serial interval is always positive, assuming infectiousness depends only on time since symptom onset is equivalent to assuming that the serial interval and generation time distributions are identical.
source: If the serial interval is always positive, which is not the case for COVID-19 (Du et al., 2020), this is equivalent to assuming that the serial interval and generation time distributions are identical (Lehtinen et al., 2021; Cori et al., 2013; Britton and Scalia Tomba, 2019).
evidence: This is a theoretical relationship supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The serial interval is not always positive for COVID-19.
source: If the serial interval is always positive, which is not the case for COVID-19 (Du et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study showing negative serial intervals.

claim: The mechanistic approach provides an improved fit to data compared to the Ferretti model.
source: However, as we have demonstrated, our mechanistic approach provides an improved fit to data compared to that model.
evidence: This is supported by the AIC comparison showing the variable infectiousness model (ΔAIC = 0) fits better than the Ferretti model (ΔAIC = 5.1).

claim: The mechanistic method is useful for parameterising population-scale compartmental epidemic forecasting models.
source: In addition, our method is useful for parameterising population-scale compartmental epidemic forecasting models, since the time periods derived using our approach correspond naturally to compartments (Hart et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method with a citation to relevant work.

claim: An assumption underlying the E/P/I structure of the best-fitting variable infectiousness model is that infectiousness may change when individuals develop symptoms.
source: It should be noted that an assumption underlying the 'E/P/I' structure of the best-fitting variable infectiousness model (Figure 1B, right, solid line) is that infectiousness may change when individuals develop symptoms.
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the model structure.

claim: In practice, behavioural changes may not occur immediately after symptoms appear, particularly if initial symptoms are mild or non-specific.
source: However, in practice behavioural changes may not occur immediately after symptoms appear, particularly if initial symptoms are mild or non-specific.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about real-world behavior based on general knowledge.

claim: A delay between symptom onset and a change in infectiousness could in principle be incorporated into the mechanistic framework by adding an additional stage of infection.
source: A delay between symptom onset and a change in infectiousness could in principle be incorporated into our mechanistic framework by adding an additional stage of infection.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about possible model extensions.

claim: The estimates were obtained using data collected early in the COVID-19 pandemic (January–March 2020).
source: One caveat of this study is that our estimates were obtained using data collected early in the COVID-19 pandemic (January–March 2020).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study regarding the temporal scope of the data.

claim: Shorter serial intervals may have been over-represented in the dataset because local case numbers were increasing in some locations where data were collected.
source: Since local case numbers were then increasing in locations where some (although not all) of the data were collected (Ferretti et al., 2020b), shorter serial intervals may have been over-represented in the dataset (Britton and Scalia Tomba, 2019).
evidence: This is a potential bias inferred from epidemic dynamics theory, supported by citations.

claim: Studies from China have indicated a shortening of the generation time over time due to non-pharmaceutical interventions.
source: On the other hand, studies from China have indicated a shortening of the generation time (Sun et al., 2021) and serial interval (Ali et al., 2020) over time due to non-pharmaceutical interventions
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies from China.

claim: Studies from China have indicated a shortening of the serial interval over time due to non-pharmaceutical interventions.
source: On the other hand, studies from China have indicated a shortening of the generation time (Sun et al., 2021) and serial interval (Ali et al., 2020) over time due to non-pharmaceutical interventions
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies from China.

claim: Differences in isolation policies are likely to affect predictions of the contribution of presymptomatic transmission.
source: Differences in isolation policies are also likely to affect predictions of the contribution of presymptomatic transmission (Casey et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: The study did not explicitly account for isolation policies already in place when the transmission pair data were collected.
source: We did not explicitly account for isolation policies already in place when the transmission pair data were collected, potentially lowering the estimated effectiveness of isolating symptomatic hosts.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the study methodology.

claim: Not accounting for existing isolation policies potentially lowers the estimated effectiveness of isolating symptomatic hosts.
source: We did not explicitly account for isolation policies already in place when the transmission pair data were collected, potentially lowering the estimated effectiveness of isolating symptomatic hosts.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential impact of a methodological limitation.

claim: The emergence of novel variants may have affected the generation time.
source: More recently, the emergence of novel variants may also have affected the generation time, although their impact is not yet fully clear (Davies et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential effects of variants, with a citation noting uncertainty.

claim: The impact of novel variants on the generation time is not yet fully clear.
source: More recently, the emergence of novel variants may also have affected the generation time, although their impact is not yet fully clear (Davies et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation indicating ongoing uncertainty.

claim: Using a novel mechanistic approach in combination with data from SARS-CoV-2 infector–infectee pairs indicates that a higher proportion of transmissions occur prior to symptoms than predicted by existing methods.
source: In summary, using a novel mechanistic approach in combination with data from SARS-CoV-2 infector–infectee pairs to infer key epidemiological quantities indicates that a higher proportion of transmissions occur prior to symptoms than predicted by existing methods.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the data analysis results.

claim: A significant proportion of presymptomatic transmissions arise immediately before symptom onset.
source: A significant proportion of these transmissions arise immediately before symptom onset.
evidence: This is supported by the TOST distribution results showing concentration around symptom onset.

claim: Combining isolation of symptomatic hosts with contact tracing and isolation of presymptomatic infected contacts is valuable even if the contact elicitation window is short.
source: This shows that, while the impact of isolation of symptomatic hosts alone may be limited, combining this with contact tracing and isolation of presymptomatic infected contacts is valuable even if the contact elicitation window is short.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the contact tracing effectiveness calculations.

claim: The use and refinement of contact tracing programmes in countries worldwide is of clear public health importance.
source: The use and refinement of contact tracing programmes in countries worldwide is therefore of clear public health importance.
evidence: This is a policy recommendation inferred from the study findings.

claim: In the main analyses, the incubation period was assumed to follow a Gamma distribution with shape parameter 5.807 and scale parameter 0.948.
source: In our main analyses, the incubation period was assumed to follow a Gamma distribution with shape parameter 5.807 and scale parameter 0.948 (Lauer et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice with a citation to the source of the parameter values.

claim: The assumed incubation period corresponds to a mean of 5.5 days and a standard deviation of 2.3 days.
source: This corresponds to a mean incubation period of 5.5 days and a standard deviation of 2.3 days.
evidence: This is calculated from the Gamma distribution parameters.

claim: An alternative Gamma distributed incubation period with a mean of 5.3 days and a standard deviation of 3.2 days was also used to test robustness.
source: However, to demonstrate that our main conclusions are robust to the exact incubation period distribution used, we also repeated our analyses using an alternative, more dispersed, Gamma distributed incubation period with a mean of 5.3 days and a standard deviation of 3.2 days (Linton et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a sensitivity analysis with a citation to the source of alternative parameter values.

claim: In the independent transmission and symptoms model, the infectiousness of each host at a given time since infection is assumed to be independent of their incubation period.
source: In this model, the infectiousness of each host at a given time since infection is assumed to be independent of their incubation period
evidence: This describes a key assumption of one of the models.

claim: In the mechanistic model, each infection was divided into three stages: latent (E), presymptomatic infectious (P), and symptomatic infectious (I).
source: In our mechanistic approach, we divided each infection into three stages: latent (E), presymptomatic infectious (P), and symptomatic infectious (I).
evidence: This describes the structure of the mechanistic model.

claim: In the mechanistic model, the stage durations were assumed to be independent.
source: The stage durations were assumed to be independent, and infectiousness was assumed to be constant over the duration of each stage.
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the mechanistic model.

claim: In the mechanistic model, infectiousness was assumed to be constant over the duration of each stage.
source: The stage durations were assumed to be independent, and infectiousness was assumed to be constant over the duration of each stage.
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the mechanistic model.

claim: In the mechanistic model, the durations of each stage were assumed to follow Gamma distributions.
source: We further assumed that the durations of each stage followed Gamma distributions
evidence: This describes a modeling assumption.

claim: Data augmentation MCMC was used to account for uncertainty in exact symptom onset times within the day of onset.
source: To account for uncertainty in the exact symptom onset times within the day of onset (and so avoid imparting bias by fitting continuous-time models to discrete-time symptom onset data), we fitted the models to the data using data augmentation MCMC (Thompson, 2020, Ferguson et al., 2005, Cauchemez et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the statistical methodology with citations supporting the approach.

claim: The MCMC chain was run for 2.5 million steps, of which the first 500,000 were discarded as burn-in.
source: The chain was run for 2.5 million steps, of which the first 500,000 were discarded as burn-in.
evidence: This describes the computational details of the MCMC procedure.

claim: Three parameters were estimated for the variable infectiousness and Ferretti models.
source: where three parameters were estimated for the variable infectiousness and Ferretti models, and two parameters for the constant infectiousness and independent transmission and symptoms models.
evidence: This describes the number of free parameters in each model.

claim: Two parameters were estimated for the constant infectiousness and independent transmission and symptoms models.
source: where three parameters were estimated for the variable infectiousness and Ferretti models, and two parameters for the constant infectiousness and independent transmission and symptoms models.
evidence: This describes the number of free parameters in each model.

claim: The study was funded by the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC).
source: Funding:Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract.
